Constitutional Mandate for Budgets
Under Article 202 of the Constitution, the Governor shall in respect of every financial
year cause to be laid before the House of the Legislature of the State a statement of
the estimated receipts and expenditure of the State for that year, known as the
"Annual Financial Statement" or Budget.
CHAPTER 5: THE MAHARASHTRA
TREASURY RULES (MTR)
The Treasury Rules outline the procedures for the receipt, custody, and withdrawal
of money from the government account. Treasuries are the primary units of the
State's accounting system.
5.1 Function of Treasuries
Treasuries and Sub-Treasuries in Maharashtra function as the focal points for
government financial transactions. Their primary duties include:
Receiving government dues and crediting them to the correct receipt heads.
Scrutinizing bills presented by DDOs to ensure they are in order and covered by
financial sanctions and budget provisions.
Making payments on behalf of the government.
Maintaining daily accounts and compiling them for submission to the
Accountant General (AG).
5.2 Treasury Code Provisions
The Maharashtra Treasury Code explicitly prohibits the withdrawal of money from
the treasury unless it is required for immediate disbursement. Drawing money to
prevent the lapse of budget grants at the end of the financial year is strictly
forbidden and constitutes a severe financial irregularity.

CHAPTER 7: RECEIPTS AND REVENUES
Government revenues arise primarily from taxes (like SGST, Stamp Duty, State
Excise) and non-tax sources (fees, fines, user charges). The financial rules stipulate
stringent guidelines for handling these receipts.
7.1 Assessment and Collection
It is the duty of the Revenue Department and other concerned authorities to ensure
that all government dues are assessed correctly, collected promptly, and paid into
the treasury immediately. No amount collected on behalf of the government can be
kept out of the government account or utilized for departmental expenditure
without specific legislative authorization.
7.2 Remittance to the Treasury
Detailed rules govern the transit of cash from the point of collection to the treasury
or the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) / State Bank of India (SBI). Receipts must be
issued for all moneys received, and a Cash Book must be maintained and closed
daily.
CHAPTER 8: EXPENDITURE AND
PAYMENT CONTROL
Expenditure from public funds is subject to a multi-layered system of checks and
balances.
8.1 Pre-requisites for Expenditure
Before any government money is spent, the following conditions must be satisfied:
Budget Provision: Funds must be available under the relevant Head of
Account.
Administrative Approval: The competent authority must have approved the
necessity of the work or service.
Technical Sanction: In the case of public works, a competent engineering
authority must approve the technical estimates.
Financial Sanction: The authority with delegated financial powers must issue a
formal order sanctioning the expenditure.
8.2 Re-appropriation of Funds
Re-appropriation is the transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another
within the same grant. The rules strictly define who can authorize re-appropriation.
Importantly, funds cannot be re-appropriated from a "Voted" head to a "Charged"
head, or to meet expenditure on a "New Service" without legislative approval.
Government e-Marketplace (GeM)
To streamline procurement, the State Government has adopted the central GeM
portal. Departments are instructed to procure standard common-use items directly
through GeM, bypassing traditional tendering for smaller amounts to ensure speed
and efficiency.
CHAPTER 10: INVENTORY AND STORES
MANAGEMENT
Once procured, physical assets and stores must be managed securely to prevent
theft, loss, or deterioration.
10.1 Custody and Verification
The rules require that:
All items received must be recorded in the Dead Stock Register or Consumables
Register.
The officer-in-charge is personally responsible for the custody of stores.
A physical verification of all stores must be conducted at least once a year by an
officer independent of the custodian.
10.2 Disposal of Obsolete Stores
Stores that become unserviceable, obsolete, or surplus must be disposed of
promptly to free up space and recover residual value. A competent authority must
declare the items as "unserviceable" based on the recommendations of a survey
committee, after which they are usually auctioned.
CHAPTER 11: ESTABLISHMENT,
SALARIES, AND PENSIONS
A significant portion of the State's expenditure goes towards the salaries,
allowances, and pensions of its employees. These are governed by the Maharashtra
Civil Services (MCS) Rules.
11.1 Pay and Allowances
The drawing of salaries requires careful maintenance of service books. The DDO
must ensure that pay bills are prepared accurately, incorporating correct
deductions for GPF/NPS, Income Tax, and Professional Tax. Annual increments must
be supported by appropriate sanction orders.
11.2 Pension Rules
The Maharashtra Civil Services (Pension) Rules govern the retirement benefits of
state employees. For employees joining on or after November 1, 2005, the state has
adopted the National Pension System (NPS), which fundamentally shifts the liability
from a defined benefit to a defined contribution model. The timely settlement of
terminal benefits (Gratuity, Commutation, Pension) is highly prioritized in the
financial rules.
CHAPTER 12: ADVANCES AND LOANS
TO GOVERNMENT SERVANTS
The State government provides certain advances to its employees, which are
categorized as interest-bearing and non-interest-bearing advances.
12.1 Types of Advances
Interest-Bearing Advances: These include House Building Advance (HBA),
Motor Car/Motorcycle Advance, and Computer Advance. These require a
minimum length of service and are subject to maximum limits based on basic
Non-Interest-Bearing Advances: These include Festival Advance (typically
granted during Diwali or other major festivals) and advances for traveling
allowance (TA) on tour or transfer.
12.2 Recovery and Accounting
Advances must be recovered from the employee's salary in prescribed monthly
installments. The DDO is strictly responsible for ensuring that recoveries begin
promptly as per the sanction order and that the principal is recovered before the
interest.
CHAPTER 13: GRANTS-IN-AID AND
LOCAL FUND ACCOUNTS
The State Government transfers significant funds to local bodies (Zilla Parishads,
Panchayat Samitis, Gram Panchayats, and Municipal Corporations) as well as non-
governmental organizations (NGOs) through Grants-in-Aid.
13.1 Conditions for Grants
Financial rules mandate that grants can only be released if specific conditions are
The grantee institution must be legally constituted.
The funds must be used specifically for the purpose they were sanctioned.
The grantee must maintain audited statements of accounts.
A "Utilization Certificate" (UC) must be submitted by the grantee. Subsequent
grants cannot be released if UCs for previous grants are pending.
13.2 Zilla Parishad Finances
The finances of Zilla Parishads in Maharashtra are governed by the Maharashtra
Zilla Parishads and Panchayat Samitis Account Code. Funds received from the State
Government under various schemes are deposited in the District Fund, and their
withdrawal and expenditure mirror the State's Treasury rules.
CHAPTER 14: CONTINGENCY FUND
RULES
The Maharashtra Contingency Fund is established under Article 267(2) of the
Constitution. It is a corpus held by the Governor, operated by the Finance
Department.
14.1 Operation of the Fund
The fund is strictly used to meet unforeseen, emergent expenditures that cannot
wait for the State Legislature's approval. For example, immediate relief measures
for natural calamities (floods, droughts) often draw from this fund.
14.2 Recoupment
Any advance taken from the Contingency Fund must be recouped by obtaining
supplementary grants from the State Legislature in its next session. The advance is
an interim measure, not a permanent source of funding.
CHAPTER 15: AUDIT AND FINANCIAL
ACCOUNTABILITY
Audit is the final and most crucial step in the financial cycle, ensuring
accountability and adherence to rules.
15.1 Statutory Audit
The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India conducts the statutory audit of
the Maharashtra Government's finances. The CAG produces several reports
annually:
Finance Accounts: The comprehensive accounts of the State's receipts and
disbursements.
Appropriation Accounts: A comparison of actual expenditure against the
budget grants voted by the Legislature, highlighting excesses or savings.
Audit Reports: Highlighting instances of financial irregularities, wasteful
expenditure, and performance audits of major schemes.
15.2 Public Accounts Committee (PAC)
The CAG's reports are laid before the State Legislature and subsequently examined
by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The PAC calls upon the Principal
Secretaries of the concerned departments to explain the irregularities pointed out
by the CAG. The PAC's recommendations carry significant weight, and the executive
must submit Action Taken Reports (ATRs).
CHAPTER 16: DEFALCATIONS, LOSSES,
AND WRITE-OFFS
Despite rigorous controls, financial losses can occur due to fraud, negligence, or
natural causes.
16.1 Reporting of Losses
The Maharashtra Financial Rules require that any loss of public money, stores, or
other property due to defalcation, fraud, or negligence must be reported
immediately to the immediate superior, the Head of the Department, and the
Accountant General, even if the loss has been made good.
16.2 Investigation and Recovery
An immediate departmental inquiry must be instituted. The primary goal is to
recover the loss from the responsible official. Under the rules, the official's pension/
gratuity can also be withheld to make good the loss.
16.3 Write-Off
If the loss is deemed irrecoverable after all avenues are exhausted, the competent
authority may sanction a "write-off." The power to write off losses is strictly
delegated, with larger amounts requiring the direct approval of the Finance
Department.
CHAPTER 17: DELEGATION OF
FINANCIAL POWERS
To ensure smooth administration without bureaucratic bottlenecks, the Finance
Department delegates specific financial powers to Administrative Departments,
Heads of Departments, and Subordinate Officers under the 'Delegation of Financial
Powers Rules' (DFPR).
17.1 Limits and Restrictions
These powers cover areas like sanctioning works, purchasing stores, condemning
obsolete items, and sanctioning leave/advances. The powers are subject to financial
limits. Any expenditure exceeding the delegated limit must be referred to the
Finance Department for concurrence.
CHAPTER 18: E-GOVERNANCE AND
FINANCIAL MODERNIZATION
In recent years, the Government of Maharashtra has aggressively modernized its
financial administration using Information Technology.
18.1 Key IT Initiatives
Sevaarth: The centralized payroll system for all government employees.
Koshwahini: The portal providing real-time data on the flow of funds in the
state exchequer, integrating treasuries, banks, and the AG.
BDS (Budget Distribution System): Electronic distribution of budget grants
from Controlling Officers to DDOs, eliminating physical delays.
E-Kuber (RBI): Integration of state treasury payments directly with the RBI's
Core Banking Solution for real-time electronic fund transfers (NEFT/RTGS) to
beneficiaries.
These systems ensure that financial rules are hardcoded into software logic,
preventing unauthorized drawals and ensuring strict budgetary control.
Conclusion
The financial laws and rules of the Government of Maharashtra represent a delicate
balance between facilitating unhindered public service delivery and maintaining
rigid control over public money. Adherence to the Maharashtra Financial Rules,
Treasury Rules, and the principles of propriety is not merely an administrative
requirement, but a constitutional duty owed to the citizens of the State.
